title: Hudson x David weekly
notes_markdown:
### Repo setup (started this week)

- Monorepo decided: `apps/web`, `workers/importers`, `packages/types`
- Shared `SourceItem` type: id, source, source_id, title, created_at, modified_at, content_hash, parts[]
- One importer per source; each yields items, never writes to the DB directly
- CI: typecheck + importer fixtures on every PR; no deploy pipeline yet

### Importer order

1. Claude export (JSON) — David has his own export to test on
2. ChatGPT export — conversation tree flattening needed (branches from edited messages)
3. Zotero (local sqlite + storage folder)
4. Local PDFs (watch ~/Downloads and ~/Desktop/papers)
5. Google Drive — later, OAuth review takes time

### Dedupe design (first cut)

- Exact: sha256 over normalized bytes → same item, merge parts
- Near: title + first-page text similarity > 0.9 → "possible duplicate" badge, never auto-merge
- Keep both source paths so the trail can say "found in Zotero and Downloads"

### Debrief from Marcus

- Retention question stuck with both of us: need weekly users, not a launch
- Follow-up memo sent Friday; Marcus replied he'll try the research-ops intro

### Action items

- [ ] David — Claude + ChatGPT importers with fixtures by Fri
- [ ] Hudson — Zotero importer spike; read the sqlite schema
- [ ] Hudson — Berkeley research-chat sign-up form + outreach email draft
- [ ] David — write the dedupe rules down as a doc in the repo

transcript.text: Is it on? The little — yeah okay, it's going.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Granola's on. Okay. Repos!
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Repos. So I made the org repos this morning. Went with the monorepo.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Thank god. I didn't want to have the, uh, the four-repo argument.
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Three folders. apps slash web, workers slash importers, packages slash types. Types is the important one.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: What's in it?
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Basically one type right now, SourceItem. id, source, source id, title, created, modified, content hash, and parts. Parts is the list of files, because some things are multi-file. Like a Zoom meeting folder is one item with ten files.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Do we have Zoom?
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: No, it's just an example. Like an email thread too. One thread, many messages.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Got it. And the importers just produce those?
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Yeah. That's the rule. An importer yields items. It never touches the database. Then one ingestion step writes them, does dedupe, all that.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: I like that because then we can test an importer with just files.
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: That's the plan. Fixtures. I'll put my own Claude export in there, scrubbed.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Scrubbed how?
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Like, I'll cut it down to, um, twenty conversations that are boring. Nothing personal. CI runs the importers on the fixtures and checks the counts.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Okay. Order?
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Claude first, because I have the export and it's clean JSON. Then ChatGPT, which is annoying because it's a tree.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: A tree?
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: When you edit a message in ChatGPT it branches. The export keeps all the branches. So you have to pick the path that's, like, the current one. Mapping, current node, walk the parents.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Oh that's gross.
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: It's fine, it's twenty lines. Then Zotero. Then local PDFs, like watching Downloads and the papers folder on the desktop. Drive last because the OAuth review thing takes weeks.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: I can take Zotero. I want to read the sqlite schema anyway.
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Please. It's — there's a storage folder with random eight-character keys and the PDFs live in there. The sqlite tells you which key is which item.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Okay. And dedupe. You said you'd write rules.
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: I have a first cut. Exact match is sha256 of the bytes. Same bytes, same item, we merge the parts.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Normalized how? PDFs have metadata that changes.
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Uh, good point. Hmm. For PDFs maybe hash the extracted text instead of the bytes? Because Zotero sometimes rewrites the file.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Does it?
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: I think when you annotate. I'm not sure. I'll check.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Okay, and the near-duplicate thing?
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Title plus first-page text, similarity over point nine, we show a badge. "Possible duplicate." We never auto-merge. That's what we agreed.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Suggest don't merge.
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Suggest don't merge. And the thing I actually think is cool, we keep both paths. So the trail can say "you have this paper in Zotero and in Downloads," which is kind of useful by itself.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: That's a feature honestly. "You have this in three places."
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Ha. Yeah. Okay. Marcus.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Marcus. So he replied to the memo Saturday. Short. "Thanks, will try the research-ops intro, talk in October."
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: That's fine. That's — what we expected.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: The retention thing is stuck in my head though.
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Mine too. Like he's right. I don't actually know if I'd use it in week four.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Do you use it now?
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: It doesn't exist now! It's three folders.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Fair, fair.
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: But, like, the honest answer is we need people using it weekly before anything. Which means the Berkeley chats matter more than I thought.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: I'm doing the sign-up form today. And an outreach email. Can you look at the email before it goes out?
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Yeah, send it to me. Don't make it sound like a pitch.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: It's "we're curious how you keep track of ideas, thirty minutes, we'll buy coffee."
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Perfect. Do we have twenty names?
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Eleven. Lena gave us two. Priya Raman's on it, the education-HCI person.
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Oh nice, she's great, I've read her stuff. Okay.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Anything else?
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Um. The camera-ready went in, by the way. I didn't say. The fourteenth, on time.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: You did say. You said it like four times.
transcript.speaker: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman

transcript.text: Did I? Okay. I'm just relieved. Okay, I'm going to go write the ChatGPT tree thing.
transcript.speaker: Me

transcript.text: Go walk the parents.
